passage: In the school counsellor's small office, Abhinav's mother twisted the strap of her bag. 'Since his Nani died, he asks the same questions every night. Will you die? Will I die? Where is she? And yesterday I found him burying his toy car in a flowerpot and saying prayers. Is something wrong with him?' Mr Irfan, the counsellor, listened. 'This is very common. Repeating questions and playing it out is how children his age make sense of a loss. Short, honest answers help more than changing the subject.' He paused. 'If it keeps going or worries you, we can talk again, and the doctor too.' She let go of the strap. 'So I don't have to stop him?' 'You can just sit with him.'

qa.q: Where did Abhinav's mother find him burying his toy car?
qa.a: She found him burying it in a flowerpot.

qa.q: What does the mother twisting her bag strap suggest?
qa.a: She is anxious and afraid that her son's repeated questions and play mean something is wrong.

qa.q: What advice did Mr Irfan give, and why does it help?
qa.a: To give short, honest, patient answers rather than distract him, because repeating and playing is how children make sense of a loss.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel if his mother kept changing the subject instead?
qa.a: He might feel his questions are wrong or scary, and be left more alone and confused with his grief.

grounding: A mother worries about her grieving son's repeated questions and burial play, and a counsellor explains it is usually normal and honest answers help.

passage: I'm Sunaina, and I'm writing down what I've seen in Vikas since his Dadu died, because I'm scared I'm missing something. Every evening at seven, the time Dadu used to call, he checks my phone. Twice this week he asked, 'But where exactly is Dadu now?' I said, 'He died, beta. His body stopped, and he can't come back.' He nodded, then asked again the next day. Yesterday I saw him make a garland of paper flowers and lay it on Dadu's chair. I don't know what goes on in his head. At first I tried distracting him with cartoons. It didn't help. Now I just answer, simply, every time he asks. He seems calmer afterwards.

qa.q: What time does Vikas check his mother's phone every evening?
qa.a: At seven, the time Dadu used to call.

qa.q: Why is Sunaina scared, and what shows it?
qa.a: She worries his repeated questions and garland-making mean something is wrong; she even writes it all down in case she's missing something.

qa.q: Which approach seems to help Vikas more, and why?
qa.a: Answering simply and honestly every time, rather than distracting him with cartoons, because it lets him make sense of the loss and he seems calmer afterwards.

qa.q: What might Vikas be looking for when he checks the phone at seven?
qa.a: He may half-expect Dadu's call, a sign that he is still searching and slowly learning the calls won't come 🤍.

grounding: A mother records her grieving son's repeated questions and ritual play, fears it is unhealthy, and finds short honest answers help more than distraction.

passage:
Week one: Rashmi noticed Kashish asking at every meal, "Is Nanu in the ground? Is he cold?" Rashmi said, "Eat your food," and changed the subject. Kashish went quiet.
Week two: Rashmi found Kashish in the garden burying her doll in a shoebox and singing. Rashmi's heart lurched. Was this normal? She phoned her friend, a school counsellor, who said it usually is, and suggested short, honest answers.
Week three: At dinner Kashish asked again. Rashmi put down her spoon. "Nanu died. His body doesn't feel cold any more. It's sad, and you can ask me anytime." Kashish nodded, and then asked for more rice.

qa.q: What was Kashish burying in the garden?
qa.a: Her doll, in a shoebox.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when her heart lurched in week two?
qa.a: She felt worried and anxious, afraid the play meant something was wrong.

qa.q: What change did Rashmi make in week three, and why did it help?
qa.a: She gave a short, honest answer and invited more questions, instead of changing the subject.

qa.q: What is it like for Kashish when her question is finally answered?
qa.a: Kashish seems settled and reassured, nodding and asking for more rice.

grounding: Shows a mother worried by her child's repeated questions and funeral play, learning that short honest answers help more than distraction.

passage:
Farhan, you're worried about your boy asking questions? Let me tell you about my Nikhil, years ago. When his Papa died, Nikhil was eight.
For weeks he asked, "Where did Papa go?" morning and night. He made his toy soldiers carry a matchbox, very slowly, across the floor. A funeral. I was frightened, Farhan. I thought he was going mad with grief. I kept saying, "Go and play outside, beta."
Then our old doctor told me, "Rukmini, he's working it out. Answer him." So I did. Short and true. "Papa died. He isn't coming back. We miss him."
The questions slowed. The matchbox went back in the drawer. And Nikhil started telling me stories about his Papa instead.

qa.q: What did Nikhil's toy soldiers carry?
qa.a: A matchbox.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when Nikhil played the funeral?
qa.a: She felt frightened and anxious, fearing he was going mad with grief.

qa.q: In the story, what turning point changed how Rukmini helped Nikhil?
qa.a: The doctor's advice to answer him, after which she gave short, true answers instead of sending him outside.

qa.q: How might Nikhil have felt once his mother answered honestly?
qa.a: Nikhil probably felt less confused and safer, since his questions slowed and he began telling stories about his Papa.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling her worry at her son's repeated questions and funeral play, and learning to answer honestly.

passage:
Their one-room flat in Dharavi was crowded with visitors all week, and Pallavi had barely slept since her husband's funeral. So when Jeevan asked, for the tenth time that day, "Where is Papa now?", she snapped, "Stop asking!"
Jeevan went silent. That night she found him under the bed, lying still with his arms crossed, eyes shut. "I'm being Papa," he whispered.
Pallavi's heart pounded. Was this normal? The next morning she asked the school counsellor, who said children often play out a funeral and repeat questions, and that short honest answers help.
That evening Jeevan asked again. Pallavi sat down beside him. "Papa died. He can't come back. I'm sad too. You can ask me anytime."

qa.q: Where did Pallavi find Jeevan that night?
qa.a: Under the bed, lying still with his arms crossed.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when she found Jeevan under the bed?
qa.a: She felt frightened and anxious, her heart pounding, wondering if his play was unhealthy.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do the next day that helped?
qa.a: She asked the school counsellor and then answered Jeevan honestly and patiently, inviting more questions.

qa.q: What is it like for Jeevan when his mother snaps at him?
qa.a: He goes silent and may feel scared and alone, with his questions shut away.

grounding: Shows a tired grieving mother worried by her son's repeated questions and funeral play, then answering honestly after advice.

passage: From the kitchen door of their third-floor flat in Pune, Trisha watched her daughter. Ira, nine, had set two dolls on the sofa and laid a white dupatta over one. "Now we say goodbye to Daadi," Ira told them, very seriously. It was the fourth time this week. At dinner she had asked, again, whether Daadi could feel cold. Trisha's stomach tightened. Was this normal? Should she hide the dolls, change the topic, buy a new game? That night she phoned her sister, a school teacher, who listened and said, "Maybe she's working it out the only way she can. Just answer her, short and true." Next morning, when Ira asked again, Trisha sat down beside her. "No, beta. Daadi can't feel cold anymore. Nothing hurts her now."

qa.q: What did Ira lay over one of the dolls?
qa.a: A white dupatta.

qa.q: What was Trisha worried about as she watched the doll play?
qa.a: She was anxious that Ira's repeated questions and funeral play were unhealthy, and unsure whether to stop them.

qa.q: Why does the sister's advice help?
qa.a: Answering short and true lets Ira keep working through the loss, which helps more than hiding the dolls or changing the topic.

qa.q: How might Ira feel when Trisha sits down and answers?
qa.a: Ira likely feels comforted and taken seriously, getting a short, true answer instead of silence.

grounding: Shows a parent worried by a grieving child's repeated questions and funeral play, and learning that short, honest answers help more than distraction.
